A line intersects the circle $\|y-x\|^2=r^2$ in at most two points: parameterizing the line as $y=a+tv$ gives a nonzero quadratic equation in $t$. Hence no three of the sites on the circle are collinear. For any one such site $p$, the tangent line at $p$ supports the disk and meets the circle only at $p$; therefore $p$ cannot be a convex combination of the other circle sites. If its affine dimension is one, sort by the first varying coordinate (use $x$ if it varies, otherwise $y$) and take the chain joining consecutive sites; this is the lower-dimensional output and contains no triangles.

Its 1-skeleton is the graph with these sites as vertices and all triangle sides as edges; it is connected. The bounded faces of this plane graph are exactly the chosen triangles, and its one unbounded face is the exterior of the convex hull. $$V(p)=\{x\in\mathbb R^2:\|x-p\|^2\le\|x-q\|^2\text{ for every site }q\}.$$

Their interior angles sum to $(h-2)\pi$, because a convex $h$-gon is divided into $h-2$ triangles by diagonals from one corner. Each of the other $k-h$ boundary sites has straight angle $\pi$. Counting all triangle angles gives $\pi T=2\pi(n-k)+(h-2)\pi+(k-h)\pi=(2n-k-2)\pi$, hence $T=2n-2-k$.

Count incidences between triangle sides and edges. Each triangle contributes three. An interior edge has one triangle on each of its two local sides; a hull edge has exactly one incident triangle inside the convex hull. Since the hull boundary has $k$ sites, it has $k$ subdivided boundary edges. Thus $3T=2(E-k)+k=2E-k$.
Substituting the value of $T$ from step 1.1 into step 1.2 gives $E=3n-3-k$. Consequently $n-E+T=n-(3n-3-k)+(2n-2-k)=1$, proving both identities.

Each triangle has at most three input vertices, so uniformity of $p_r$ gives $\mathbb E[k_r(q,p_r)\mid S_r]\le3k_r(q)/r$. Count first the triangles in the final Delaunay triangulations $T_r$ that are created at a stage; for such a triangle $\Gamma$, let $K(\Gamma)$ be the set of later input sites strictly inside its circumdisk. If a visited node is destroyed by a face split, it is the old Delaunay triangle $\Gamma$ being split; the query lies inside it and hence in $K(\Gamma)$. If it is destroyed by a flip, the flip removes an old Delaunay triangle $\Gamma$ whose circumdisk contains the inserted site, together with one triangle incident to that site. In unweighted mode, a duplicate means equal coordinates; collapse each such class to its least identifier. In weighted mode, a duplicate means an equal coordinate-weight pair; collapse only equal pairs to the least identifier. Equal coordinates with unequal weights remain distinct weighted sites.

The unweighted deduplicated set keeps, for each coordinate value $p$, the entry with least identifier among entries at $p$, and records each discarded identifier in a duplicate map. The weighted deduplicated set keeps the least identifier for each exact pair $(p,w)$ and records only repeated pairs in its duplicate map. A weighted computation retains different weights at the same coordinate; their power values are compared by the ordinary power-distance rule, so a dominated weight may be hidden.

Throughout this page, $\mathbb R$ is a commutative field with $1>0$, a total order compatible with addition and multiplication, and the least-upper-bound property. Let $\mathbb D=\{m2^e:m,e\in\mathbb Z\}$ be its dyadic subfield. For $d\in\{2,3\}$, a nonempty finite indexed site list is a finite list
$$S=((\iota_1,p_1,w_1),\ldots,(\iota_N,p_N,w_N)),$$
where every $\iota_i\in\mathbb Z$ is a distinct stable identifier, every $p_i\in\mathbb D^d$, and each optional weight $w_i$ is either absent (meaning $0$) or belongs to $\mathbb D$. In unweighted mode, a duplicate means equal coordinates; collapse each such class to its least identifier. In weighted mode, a duplicate means an equal coordinate-weight pair; collapse only equal pairs to the least identifier. Equal coordinates with unequal weights remain distinct weighted sites.

The unweighted deduplicated set keeps, for each coordinate value $p$, the entry with least identifier among entries at $p$, and records each discarded identifier in a duplicate map. The weighted deduplicated set keeps the least identifier for each exact pair $(p,w)$ and records only repeated pairs in its duplicate map. A weighted computation retains different weights at the same coordinate; their power values are compared by the ordinary power-distance rule, so a dominated weight may be hidden.

For a finite point set $P\subseteq\mathbb R^d$, its convex hull is the set of all finite convex combinations of points of $P$. Its affine dimension is the dimension of its affine hull. A tuple $p_0,\ldots,p_d$ is affinely independent when the vectors $p_1-p_0,\ldots,p_d-p_0$ form a basis of $\mathbb R^d$; here a basis means every vector has a unique linear expansion in those vectors. This convention makes nondegenerate simplex coordinates unique.

Use the unweighted deduplicated coordinate set of [[def-indexed-geometric-site-set]]. If its affine dimension is zero, its output is its single site. If its affine dimension is one, sort by the first varying coordinate (use $x$ if it varies, otherwise $y$) and take the chain joining consecutive sites; this is the lower-dimensional output and contains no triangles.

For affine dimension two, a **triangulation of the sites** is a finite family of nondegenerate closed triangles whose vertices are sites, whose union is the convex hull, and whose pairwise intersections are common faces. Its 1-skeleton is the graph with these sites as vertices and all triangle sides as edges; it is connected. The bounded faces of this plane graph are exactly the chosen triangles, and its one unbounded face is the exterior of the convex hull. The boundary edges of the convex hull are subdivided at every site on that boundary. A triangle is **weakly empty-circle** when no site lies strictly inside its circumdisk; other sites may lie on its boundary.

For each site $p$, its closed **Voronoi cell** is
$$V(p)=\{x\in\mathbb R^2:\|x-p\|^2\le\|x-q\|^2\text{ for every site }q\}.$$
A tie belongs to every minimizing cell. The **Delaunay graph** has one vertex for each site and an edge $pq$ exactly when $V(p)\cap V(q)$ contains a nontrivial line segment. A **Voronoi vertex** is a point belonging to at least three distinct cells. It is dual to the convex polygon of the nearest sites; [[lem-voronoi-vertex-empty-circle]] proves that those sites are vertices on one empty circle centered at that point. A **Delaunay triangulation** is a triangulation refining these polygonal Delaunay faces and having weakly empty circumdisks. In a cocircular face the triangulation need not be unique; the chosen algorithmic refinement is the fixed-universe convention of [[def-lexicographic-lift-tie-break]].

The convex-hull boundary is the boundary of the union of the triangles. An unbounded Voronoi cell corresponds to a site on that boundary. No minimum-angle or other mesh-quality condition is part of these definitions.

In the affine-dimension-two branch, after each insertion the augmented triangles are exactly the $d=2$ lower simplices of the common fixed-universe formal lift, as defined in [[lem-lower-lifted-facets-cover-the-convex-hull]]. After removing synthetic vertices, the output triangulates the input convex hull with weakly empty original circumdisks and coherent lexicographic ties. In dimensions zero and one, the algorithm returns the defined single site or consecutive chain.

For a triangulation of the convex hull of $n$ distinct planar sites with affine dimension two, let $k$ be the number of sites on the hull boundary, $T$ the number of triangles, and $E$ the number of edges. Then
$$T=2n-2-k,\qquad E=3n-3-k.$$
In particular $T<2n$ and $E<3n$.
